newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan lenders post healthy profits, outlook fuzzy.
newsitem.headline: Japan lenders post healthy profits, outlook fuzzy.

text.p: Major Japanese personal loan firms made healthy profits last business year, helped by an increase in automated telling machines and success in attracting younger clients who know little of the days when the firms were put in the same category as loan-sharks.
But analysts said on Tuesday the industry may be reaching a peak and profits in coming years may slow down.

"Consumer financers had a lot going for them up till now -- historically low bank lending rates and new customers due to an image revamp as big industry names went public," said Daiwa Institute of Research analyst, Mitsumasa Okamoto. "But it can't last forever and the signs of a slowdown are apparent."

Acom Co Ltd, the industry's second largest firm, said its parent current profits jumped 17.3 percent to 88.61 billion yen ($784 million) In the year ended March 1997. It posted a 40 percent rise in profits in 1995/96.
Current profit is a pre-tax profit which includes gains and losses made on securities investments and other non-operating activities.
Third ranked Promise Co Ltd's profits rose 11.4 percent to 67.76 billion yen ($599 million) in the past business year, after nearly 20 percent growth in the previous year.
Industry leader Takefuji Corp's parent current profit rose to 122.08 billion yen ($1.08 billion) in 1996/97, compared with 110.77 billion yen ($980 million) in the previous year.
For the current 1997/98 business year, profit growth is seen stalling at about 10 percent for most of the larger firms.

Analysts said the cost of switching over from shops with clerks to automated telling machines, which not only cut personnel costs but cultivate a new range of young clients, would be the main culprit in slowing profits.
They said the young clients, unlike those in the past, borrow to make up for small cash shortages to buy a new dress or a pair of shoes, rather than to deal with dire financial circumstances.
"The market is pretty well saturated now and in the future, it may be more difficult to find new customers," said Ayako Sato, a UBS Securities analyst.

Heightened competition is also forcing firms to cut their own lending rates, which will squeeze profit margins. Effective April 1, Acom's maximum rate has been cut to 27.375 percent from 28.47 percent per year.

Up until now, Japan's low market rates have been a big plus for the firms, which raise funds by borrowing from other financial institutions, but analysts say that it is only a matter of time before this scenario changes.

The money lenders, who mostly deal in small cash loans averaging 400,000 yen ($3,539), have recently come under fire due to a surge in personal bankruptcies. In 1996, such bankruptcies rocketed 30 percent from the previous year.

"The increase in bankruptcies cannot be linked directly with the booming business of personal loan firms, but they were known for outrageously high interest rates and hard-nosed collecting tactics in the past and are vulnerable to such news," one analyst said.
"The industry must strive to keep its image from being tarnished or else the new clients will shy away, which will be a serious depressant for profits," he added.
